headline: Today in Tech & Research
narrative_html:
Today in Tech: From SSL Stacks to Self-Driving Personalization

A roundup of today’s most urgent and intriguing technology stories: SSL library challenges, a corrective on OOP’s origins, and new AI advances in few-shot learning and personalized autonomous driving.

The SSL Stack Dilemma

The most urgent development today concerns the SSL library ecosystem, which is facing what amounts to a crisis. OpenSSL 3.0, released in September 2021, has introduced significant performance regressions in multi-threaded environments while simultaneously deprecating APIs that many projects depend on. This creates a perfect storm for organizations running high-performance infrastructure.

The performance issues aren't minor - they're substantial enough that companies may need to provision additional hardware just to maintain existing throughput levels. This has direct implications for energy consumption, carbon footprint, and operational costs. The timing couldn't be worse, as OpenSSL 1.1.1, which many prefer, is losing maintenance support.

What makes this particularly problematic is that Linux distributions have largely moved to OpenSSL 3.0 despite its limitations, since it's the designated Long-Term Support version. Organizations are now forced to choose between using increasingly unsupported older versions or accepting significant performance penalties.

Alternative SSL libraries like BoringSSL, LibreSSL, WolfSSL, and AWS-LC exist, but each comes with its own compatibility and maintenance tradeoffs. This isn't just a technical implementation detail - it affects everything from TLS protocol support to QUIC adoption, certificate management, and regulatory compliance.

The Corrective Record on OOP

In lighter but still significant news, there's a 2019 piece debunking misconceptions about Object-Oriented Programming. Contrary to some claims, Alan Kay didn't invent objects - they originated in Simula, which the Smalltalk team explicitly cited as inspiration. Kay did coin the term "Object-Oriented Programming," but the notion that OOP was primarily about message-passing rather than classes and objects appears to be a later reinterpretation.

What's particularly interesting is how the piece contextualizes Smalltalk's innovations within Kay's broader vision of personal computing. The late binding and message passing mechanisms weren't abstract computer science - they were practical solutions to make computers more accessible and resilient. In Kay's vision, users should be able to install new programs without recompiling the OS, and a person "clobbering" sound logic shouldn't crash the entire system.

This stands in contrast to Simula's creators, who were focused on simulation problems where message passing wasn't as critical. The takeaway is that OOP evolved as a synthesis of multiple perspectives addressing different problems, rather than having one "true" definition.

AI Advances in Few-Shot Learning and Autonomous Driving

Two AI papers caught attention today. First, "Latte" introduces a framework for transferring knowledge from Large Language Models to few-shot tabular learning tasks. Unlike previous approaches that either extract knowledge at test time (creating latency) or rely on text-level knowledge (leading to unreliable feature engineering), Latte extracts latent knowledge during training time.

The key innovation is that Latte enables weighted fusion of information across different feature values while reducing overfitting risk in limited-data scenarios. It's also compatible with existing unsupervised pre-training approaches and can leverage unlabeled samples to overcome limitations imposed by extremely small labeled datasets.

Meanwhile, "PADriver" tackles personalized autonomous driving using Multi-modal Large Language Models. It processes streaming frames and personalized text prompts to perform scene understanding, danger level estimation, and action decisions. The danger level assessment provides an explicit risk reference for potential actions, which corresponds to the preset personalized prompt.

The researchers have also created a benchmark called PAD-Highway based on the Highway-Env simulator, containing 250 hours of annotated video. Their experimental results suggest PADriver outperforms existing approaches and enables various driving modes.

The Common Thread

What ties today's developments together is a tension between legacy systems and emerging innovations. The SSL stack crisis exemplifies how infrastructure dependencies can create significant challenges when evolving. The OOP history reminder shows how technology narratives get simplified and distorted over time. And the AI papers demonstrate how researchers continue pushing boundaries by transferring knowledge between domains (Latte) and personalizing previously standardized systems (PADriver).

The most actionable insight might be to reassess any critical systems relying on OpenSSL 3.0 for performance-sensitive applications. The performance degradation in multi-threaded environments could be silently affecting operational costs and efficiency.

item.title: Latte: Transfering LLMs` Latent-level Knowledge for Few-shot Tabular Learning
item.summary:
Few-shot tabular learning, in which machine learning models are trained with
a limited amount of labeled data, provides a cost-effective approach to
addressing real-world challenges. The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs)
has sparked interest in leveraging their pre-trained knowledge for few-shot
tabular learning. Despite promising results, existing approaches either rely on
test-time knowledge extraction, which introduces undesirable latency, or
text-level knowledge, which leads to unreliable feature engineering. To
overcome these limitations, we propose Latte, a training-time knowledge
extraction framework that transfers the latent prior knowledge within LLMs to
optimize a more generalized downstream model. Latte enables general
knowledge-guided downstream tabular learning, facilitating the weighted fusion
of information across different feature values while reducing the risk of
overfitting to limited labeled data. Furthermore, Latte is compatible with
existing unsupervised pre-training paradigms and effectively utilizes available
unlabeled samples to overcome the performance limitations imposed by an
extremely small labeled dataset. Extensive experiments on various few-shot
tabular learning benchmarks demonstrate the superior performance of Latte,
establishing it as a state-of-the-art approach in this domain

items.why:
Based on your background and interests, "Latte: Transferring LLMs' Latent-level Knowledge for Few-shot Tabular Learning" could be a worthwhile read, but with some caveats. The paper is squarely in the intersection of LLMs, transfer learning, and practical ML applications—especially for tabular data, which is a huge real-world domain but often underserved by deep learning advances. The key novelty here is extracting *latent* (not just textual) knowledge from LLMs at training time, to improve few-shot tabular learning without the latency and reliability issues of test-time prompting or text-based feature engineering. If you’re interested in productizing LLM-powered tools for domains like analytics, business intelligence, or any workflow that touches tabular data, this is directly relevant.

However, if your primary focus is on building LLM-powered *developer* tools, agent systems, or orchestration utilities, the core technical contribution might feel a bit tangential unless you’re specifically looking to expand into ML-for-tabular-data products. The "Latte" approach is more about using LLMs as a source of generalizable knowledge to improve classic ML tasks, rather than pushing the boundaries of LLM orchestration, agent design, or human-in-the-loop systems. That said, the general idea of extracting and transferring *latent* knowledge from LLMs could inspire analogous techniques in your own domain, especially if you’re thinking about hybrid systems or new ways to leverage LLMs beyond prompt engineering.

Bottom line: If you’re hunting for major new paradigms in LLM tooling or agent architectures, this paper is probably more "interesting adjacent" than "must-read." But if you want to stay sharp on how LLMs are being used to augment other ML tasks—especially in ways that go beyond prompt-based workflows—skimming this could spark some useful ideas, or at least keep you aware of the evolving landscape. If you’re pressed for time, a quick scan of the method and results sections should tell you if there’s a direct application or inspiration for your own work.
items.overview:
"Latte: Transferring LLMs' Latent-level Knowledge for Few-shot Tabular Learning" addresses the challenge of training machine learning models on tabular data when only a small amount of labeled data is available. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated the ability to encode extensive general knowledge, prior approaches to leveraging LLMs for few-shot tabular learning have significant drawbacks. Specifically, methods that extract knowledge at test time introduce latency, and those that rely on text-level knowledge can result in unreliable feature engineering. To address these issues, the authors introduce Latte, a framework that extracts latent prior knowledge from LLMs during training, transferring it to downstream models tasked with tabular learning.

Latte operates by guiding downstream tabular learning with general knowledge distilled from LLMs at the latent representation level, rather than relying on textual outputs or prompt-based workflows. This approach facilitates a weighted fusion of information across different feature values in the tabular data, which helps mitigate overfitting—a common risk when working with limited labeled samples. Additionally, Latte is compatible with existing unsupervised pre-training paradigms, allowing it to leverage available unlabeled data to further improve performance, even when the labeled dataset is extremely small. The framework is designed to optimize for generalization, making it suitable for a variety of real-world tabular learning scenarios.

Experimental results on several few-shot tabular learning benchmarks demonstrate that Latte achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, establishing it as a state-of-the-art approach within this domain. The technical contribution is particularly relevant for applications in analytics, business intelligence, and other workflows that rely heavily on tabular data, where cost-effective and robust learning from limited labels is crucial. While the core focus is on enhancing classic machine learning tasks with LLM-derived knowledge, rather than on LLM agent design or developer tooling, the underlying technique of latent knowledge extraction may offer transferable insights for hybrid systems or other domains seeking to leverage LLMs beyond conventional prompt engineering.
items.context: Latte is a method for improving machine learning on tabular data (think spreadsheets or databases) by leveraging the internal, 'latent' knowledge of large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4. Traditionally, LLMs are used for text tasks, and their knowledge is accessed via text prompts at inference time, which can be slow and unreliable. Latte instead extracts useful representations from inside the LLM during training, transferring this knowledge directly into models designed for tabular data, especially when only a few labeled examples are available ('few-shot' learning). This approach aims to boost performance on real-world tabular tasks—common in business and analytics—without relying on prompt engineering or LLM calls at test time, making it more efficient and robust for practical ML applications.

item.title: The State of SSL Stacks
item.summary: A paper on this topic was prepared for internal use within HAProxy last year, and this version is now being shared publicly. Given the critical role of SSL in securing internet communication and the challenges presented by evolving SSL technologies, reverse proxies like HAProxy must continuously adapt their SSL strategies to maintain performance and compatibility, ensuring a secure and efficient experience for users. We are committed to providing ongoing updates on these developments.The SSL landscape has shifted dramatically in the past few years, introducing performance bottlenecks and compatibility challenges for developers. Once a reliable foundation, OpenSSL's evolution has prompted a critical reassessment of SSL strategies across the industry. For years, OpenSSL maintained its position as the de facto standard SSL library, offering long-term stability and consistent performance. The arrival of version 3.0 in September 2021 changed everything. While designed to enhance security and modularity, the new architecture introduced significant performance regressions in multi-threaded environments, and deprecated essential APIs that many external projects relied upon. The absence of the anticipated QUIC API further complicated matters for developers who had invested in its implementation.This transition posed a challenge for the entire ecosystem. OpenSSL 3.0 was designated as the Long-Term Support (LTS) version, while maintenance for the widely used 1.1.1 branch was discontinued. As a result, many Linux distributions had no practical choice but to adopt the new version despite its limitations. Users with performance-critical applications found themselves at a crossroads: continue with increasingly unsupported earlier versions or accept substantial penalties in performance and functionality.Performance testing reveals the stark reality: in some multi-threaded configurations, OpenSSL 3.0 performs significantly worse than alternative SSL libraries, forcing organizations to provision more hardware just to maintain existing throughput. This raises important questions about performance, energy efficiency, and operational costs.Examining alternatives—BoringSSL, LibreSSL, WolfSSL, and AWS-LC—reveals a landscape of trade-offs. Each offers different approaches to API compatibility, performance optimization, and QUIC support. For developers navigating the modern SSL ecosystem, understanding these trade-offs is crucial for optimizing performance, maintaining compatibility, and future-proofing their infrastructure.Functional requirementsThe functional aspects of SSL libraries determine their versatility and applicability across different software products. HAProxy’s SSL feature set was designed around the OpenSSL API, so compatibility or functionality parity is a key requirement. Modern implementations must support a range of TLS protocol versions (from legacy TLS 1.0 to current TLS 1.3) to accommodate diverse client requirements while encouraging migration to more secure protocols. Support for innovative, emerging protocols like QUIC plays a vital role in driving widespread adoption and technological breakthroughs. Certificate management functionality, including chain validation, revocation checking via OCSP and CRLs, and SNI (Server Name Indication) support, is essential for proper deployment. SSL libraries must offer comprehensive cipher suite options to meet varying security policies and compliance requirements such as PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and FIPS. Standard features like ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) for HTTP/2 support, certificate transparency validation, and stapling capabilities further expand functional requirements. Software products relying on these libraries must carefully evaluate which functional components are critical for their specific use cases while considering the overhead these features may introduce.Performance considerationsSSL/TLS operations are computationally intensive, creating significant performance challenges for software products that rely on these libraries. Handshake operations, which establish secure connections, require asymmetric cryptography that can consume substantial CPU resources, especially in high-volume environments. They also present environmental and logistical challenges alongside their computational demands. The energy consumption of cryptographic operations directly impacts the carbon footprint of digital infrastructure relying on these security protocols. High-volume SSL handshakes and encryption workloads increase power requirements in data centers, contributing to greater electricity consumption and associated carbon emissions. Performance of SSL libraries has become increasingly important as organizations pursue sustainability goals and green computing initiatives. Modern software products implement sophisticated core-awareness strategies that maximize single-node efficiency by distributing cryptographic workloads across all available CPU cores. This approach to processor saturation enables organizations to fully utilize existing hardware before scaling horizontally, significantly reducing both capital expenditure and energy consumption that would otherwise be required for additional servers. By efficiently leveraging all available cores for SSL/TLS operations, a single properly configured node can often handle the same encrypted traffic volume as multiple poorly optimized servers, dramatically reducing datacenter footprint, cooling requirements, and power consumption. These architectural improvements, when properly leveraged by SSL libraries, can deliver substantial performance improvements with minimal environmental impact—a critical consideration as encrypted traffic continues to grow exponentially across global networks.Maintenance requirementsThe maintenance burden of SSL implementations presents significant challenges for software products. Security vulnerabilities in SSL libraries require immediate attention, forcing development teams to establish robust patching processes. Software products must balance the stability of established SSL libraries against the security improvements of newer versions; this process becomes more manageable when operating system vendors provide consistent and timely updates. Documentation and expertise requirements add further complexity, as configuring SSL properly demands specialized knowledge that may be scarce within development teams. Backward compatibility concerns often complicate maintenance, as updates must protect existing functionality while implementing necessary security improvements or fixes. The complexity and risks associated with migrating to a new SSL library version often encourage product vendors to try to stick as long as possible to the same maintenance branch, preferably an LTS version provided by the operating system’s vendor. Current SSL library ecosystemOpenSSLOpenSSL has served as the industry-standard SSL library included in most operating systems for many years. A key benefit has been its simultaneous support for multiple versions over extended periods, enabling users to carefully schedule upgrades, adapt their code to accommodate new versions, and thoroughly test them before implementation.The introduction of OpenSSL 3.0 in September 2021 posed significant challenges to the stability of the SSL ecosystem, threatening its continued reliability and sustainability.This version was released nearly a year behind schedule, thus shortening the available timeframe for migrating applications to the new version. The migration process was challenging due to OpenSSL's API changes, such as the deprecation of many commonly used functions and the ENGINE API that external projects relied on. This affected solutions like the pkcs11 engine used for Hardware Security Modules (HSM) and Intel’s QAT engine for hardware crypto acceleration, forcing engines to be rewritten with the new providers API. items.overview:
"The State of SSL Stacks" provides a comprehensive examination of the evolving landscape of SSL/TLS libraries, with a particular focus on the impact of OpenSSL 3.0’s release on performance, compatibility, and maintenance for infrastructure components like reverse proxies. The paper, originally prepared for HAProxy’s internal use, details how OpenSSL’s longstanding stability and ubiquity were disrupted by the introduction of version 3.0 in September 2021. This release, intended to improve security and modularity, instead brought significant performance regressions—especially in multi-threaded environments—and deprecated widely used APIs, including the ENGINE API critical to hardware crypto acceleration and HSM integration. The lack of a QUIC API further complicated adoption for those invested in modern protocols. As OpenSSL 3.0 became the designated Long-Term Support (LTS) version and support for 1.1.1 was discontinued, many Linux distributions were forced to upgrade, leaving users with performance-critical workloads to choose between unsupported legacy versions or accepting degraded throughput and increased hardware requirements.

The paper systematically compares OpenSSL 3.0 with alternative SSL libraries such as BoringSSL, LibreSSL, WolfSSL, and AWS-LC, highlighting the trade-offs in API compatibility, performance, and protocol support, including QUIC. It outlines the functional requirements for modern SSL libraries, which must support a range of TLS versions (from 1.0 to 1.3), robust certificate management (including chain validation, revocation checking via OCSP and CRLs, and SNI), comprehensive cipher suite options for regulatory compliance (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FIPS), and features like ALPN for HTTP/2, certificate transparency, and stapling. The performance demands of SSL/TLS—particularly handshake operations and asymmetric cryptography—are emphasized, as these can create significant CPU and energy overhead in high-volume environments. The report notes that maximizing single-node efficiency through core-aware workload distribution can reduce both capital and operational costs, as well as environmental impact, by minimizing the need for additional servers and associated power consumption.

Maintenance considerations are also addressed, including the need for prompt patching of security vulnerabilities, the complexity introduced by frequent API changes, and the importance of reliable documentation and expertise. The migration to new SSL library versions is complicated by backward compatibility concerns and the desire to remain on stable, LTS-supported branches provided by OS vendors. The paper concludes that the SSL ecosystem’s stability has been challenged by OpenSSL 3.0’s delayed and disruptive release, which shortened migration timelines and required substantial adaptation from dependent projects. For organizations building or operating performance-critical infrastructure—such as reverse proxies, load balancers, or custom networking solutions—understanding these shifts and the specific capabilities and limitations of available SSL libraries is essential for maintaining secure, efficient, and sustainable services. For those working primarily with higher-level application logic or managed platforms, the immediate relevance may be lower, but awareness of these foundational changes remains useful, especially if future work involves direct SSL/TLS integration or infrastructure tooling.
items.context: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and its successor TLS (Transport Layer Security) are cryptographic protocols that secure data transmitted over networks, forming the backbone of HTTPS and other secure communications. An 'SSL stack' refers to the software libraries (like OpenSSL, BoringSSL, or LibreSSL) that implement these protocols, handling encryption, certificate validation, and secure handshakes. OpenSSL is the most widely used library, but recent major updates (notably OpenSSL 3.0) have introduced breaking changes and performance regressions, impacting systems that rely on custom or high-performance networking (such as reverse proxies, load balancers, or bespoke backend services). For most application developers using managed platforms or frameworks, SSL details are abstracted away, but for those building or maintaining infrastructure, understanding the trade-offs and current state of SSL stacks is crucial for security, compatibility, and performance.

item.title: PADriver: Towards Personalized Autonomous Driving
item.summary:
In this paper, we propose PADriver, a novel closed-loop framework for
personalized autonomous driving (PAD). Built upon Multi-modal Large Language
Model (MLLM), PADriver takes streaming frames and personalized textual prompts
as inputs. It autoaggressively performs scene understanding, danger level
estimation and action decision. The predicted danger level reflects the risk of
the potential action and provides an explicit reference for the final action,
which corresponds to the preset personalized prompt. Moreover, we construct a
closed-loop benchmark named PAD-Highway based on Highway-Env simulator to
comprehensively evaluate the decision performance under traffic rules. The
dataset contains 250 hours videos with high-quality annotation to facilitate
the development of PAD behavior analysis. Experimental results on the
constructed benchmark show that PADriver outperforms state-of-the-art
approaches on different evaluation metrics, and enables various driving modes.

items.why:
Given your background—deep technical chops, strong interest in LLMs and agent systems, and a desire to build real, marketable products—**PADriver** is probably not a must-read for you *unless* you have a specific interest in autonomous vehicles, robotics, or applying LLMs to embodied/real-world control. The paper is in the hot area of using large (multi-modal) language models for real-time, closed-loop decision-making, which is a trend worth tracking in general, but the application domain here (personalized autonomous driving) is fairly specialized. Unless you’re looking to pivot into robotics/autonomous systems, the direct technical content may not be immediately actionable for your indie dev/product ambitions.

That said, the *meta-ideas*—like using LLMs for streaming, real-time multi-modal decision-making, and the notion of "personalization" in agentic systems—*are* relevant to the broader LLM tooling and product landscape. The way they’ve structured the system (streaming frames + textual prompts → scene understanding + risk estimation + action selection) could inspire analogous architectures for interactive, user-personalized LLM apps in other domains. The closed-loop benchmarking and the emphasis on explicit risk estimation are also interesting patterns that could transfer to other agentic or workflow systems (e.g., LLM-powered assistants that need to make and justify decisions in real time).

In summary: **Skim the intro, system diagram, and maybe the experiments section for architectural inspiration and transferable ideas, but don’t feel obliged to do a deep dive unless you’re specifically interested in LLMs for embodied/real-time control.** If you’re looking for “big deal” research for the LLM product/dev space, this is more of a niche curiosity than a foundational shift—but it’s a good example of how LLMs are starting to eat more complex, real-world tasks. If you want maximum ROI for your time, you might be better off tracking papers that focus on LLM orchestration, agent frameworks, or new interaction paradigms for LLM-backed products.
items.overview:
PADriver is a closed-loop framework designed for personalized autonomous driving (PAD), leveraging a Multi-modal Large Language Model (MLLM) to process both streaming visual data (frames) and personalized textual prompts. The system operates autoaggressively, executing three core tasks in real time: scene understanding, danger level estimation, and action decision. The predicted danger level quantifies the risk associated with potential driving actions and serves as an explicit reference for selecting the final maneuver, which is tailored to the user's preset prompt. This approach enables the system to support various driving modes, adapting behavior according to individual preferences or requirements.

To evaluate PADriver, the authors introduce PAD-Highway, a closed-loop benchmark built on the Highway-Env simulator. This benchmark is designed to comprehensively assess decision-making performance within the constraints of traffic rules. The accompanying dataset comprises 250 hours of video with high-quality annotations, supporting detailed analysis of PAD behaviors and facilitating further research in this area. Experimental results demonstrate that PADriver outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches across multiple evaluation metrics, confirming its effectiveness in both decision quality and adaptability to different driving modes.

While the technical contributions of PADriver are most directly relevant to those interested in autonomous vehicles, robotics, or the application of LLMs to real-world control systems, the paper also presents meta-ideas with broader applicability. The architecture—integrating streaming multi-modal inputs, explicit risk estimation, and personalized action selection—may inform the design of interactive, user-personalized LLM applications in other domains. Additionally, the closed-loop benchmarking methodology and explicit risk estimation mechanisms could be adapted for LLM-powered assistants or agentic systems that require real-time decision-making and justification. However, for those not focused on embodied or real-time control, the primary value lies in architectural inspiration rather than immediate product development insights.
items.context: PADriver is a research project that explores how large language models (LLMs)—especially those capable of processing both text and images (multi-modal)—can be used to control autonomous vehicles in a personalized way. Traditionally, autonomous driving systems rely on specialized perception and planning modules, but PADriver instead uses LLMs to interpret streaming sensor data (like camera frames), understand the driving scene, estimate risks, and select driving actions in real time, all while adapting to user preferences. This approach is part of a broader trend of applying LLMs to real-world, embodied tasks that require continuous, closed-loop decision-making, rather than just static text generation. The paper also emphasizes explicit risk estimation and benchmarking in real-time scenarios, which are concepts that could be relevant for building interactive, decision-making LLM agents in other domains beyond robotics or autonomous vehicles.

item.title: Alan Kay Did Not Invent Objects (2019)
item.summary: People keep claiming that modern OOP languages aren’t “really OOP” because they don’t follow Alan Kay’s definition of “OOP”. I can see the logic here, even if I disagree the conclusion. More recently I’ve seen people start claiming that Kay invented objects entirely. This is factually incorrect. Alan Kay did not invent objects. They come from Simula, which the Smalltalk-72 manual cites as a major inspiration (pg 117). The famous 1981 Byte magazine issue that popularized Smalltalk and OOP explicitly says “the fundamental idea of objects, messages, and classes came from SIMULA.” It says that Simula allows users to create “object-oriented systems”, which is probably going to far but still. The Smalltalk team clearly knew about, and was inspired by, Simula’s object system. Part of the reason this is such a persistent myth is because Kay himself said it in 1998: Just a gentle reminder that I took some pains at the last OOPSLA to try to remind everyone that Smalltalk is not only NOT its syntax or the class library, it is not even about classes. I’m sorry that I long ago coined the term “objects” for this topic because it gets many people to focus on the lesser idea. And later follows that up in this interview: I mean, I made up the term “objects.” Since we did objects first, there weren’t any objects to radicalize. He later stopped claiming this but those other sources are still out there and still cited by people as fact. Alan Kay coined the term “Object-Oriented Programming” This is absolutely true. OOP was about classes and objects More recently people keep claiming that OOP “isn’t really” about classes and objects and the important bit is actually the messages. In the 1998 post, after saying how much he regrets “objects”, Kay also says that “the big idea is ‘messaging’”. He later follows up with: OOP to me means only messaging, local retention and protection and hiding of state-process, and extreme late-binding of all things. It can be done in Smalltalk and in LISP. There are possibly other systems in which this is possible, but I’m not aware of them. Early OOP definitely considered messages important, but that primarily in the service of objects. Here’s how Dan Ingalls explains OOP in his introduction of Smalltalk-76: The Smalltalk language is object oriented rather than function oriented, and this often confuses people with previous experience in computer science. For example, to evaluate <someobject>+4 means to present +4 as a message to the object. The fundamental difference is that the object is in control, not +. If <someobject> is the integer 3, then the result will be the integer 7. However, if <someobject> were the string 'Meta', the result might be Meta4. In this way, meaning rides with the objects of the system, and code remains an abstract form, merely directing the flow of communication. In “Microelectronics and the Personal Computer” Kay talks about a “message-activity” system where “each activity belongs to a family” and talks about extending activities into “viewpoints” of object relationships as the future frontier. In the Smalltalk-72 manual he says (p. 18) The central idea in writing Small talk programs, then, is to define classes which handle communication among objects in the created environment. Looking at the early sources, everybody acts as if OOP consisted of three major ideas: classes that defined protocol and implementation, objects as instances of classes, and messages as the means of communication. The idea that classes and objects were secondary to the messages comes much later. Smalltalk was the first true OOP language The ACM gave a Turing award to Dahl and Nygaard and called them “co-inventors of OOP”. The Byte magazine similarly says Simula was object-oriented, and in “The Computer Revolution hasn’t happened yet” Kay calls Sketchpad “very object-oriented”. In my opinion, this doesn’t give Smalltalk enough credit. Unlike the other systems, in Smalltalk: There were no non-object primitives. Numbers were objects. Errors were objects. Classes were objects. Messages were objects. You could pass a message to any object, including other messages. Methods and implementations were associated with the objects, not the session. The last one is the most subtle one and arguably the most important contribution, though nobody properly explains what makes it so special. In Simula, calling a missing method causes an error. This is part of the Simula spec. In Smalltalk-80, if no method matches the message, the object returns to the caller a doesNotUnderstand message by default. The calling object can choose to react to it, or just pass it along, or raise an error. A class can also override the default and do something besides return doesNotUnderstand. It also means the messaging system is independent from the object internals. The two don’t even have to be part of the same project. This means that you can do things like send messages to objects written in different languages, transmit object definitions by mail, send messages via SMS, etc. In my opinion this is where a lot of the power of “message-passing” lies, but it’s also one of the least explored aspects. Smalltalk had a surrounding context People don’t invent tools in a vacuum. They have specific situations and problems and try to find solutions to those problems. Smalltalk’s innovations and OOP are no different. Alan Kay was interested in personal computing. His work on FLEX, the Dynabook, and Smalltalk all revolve around that. In his vision, the PC would be a something totally under the user’s control, everything from core system logic to the graphic rendering tweakable and explorable at runtime. Message passing and late binding solve a lot of problems here. If a kid installs a new game, should they have to recompile the entire OS to use the new program? No: make it so that you can send any arbitrary message to any object and rely on runtime protocol-handling to fix it.1 If a person clobbers the sound logic, should the whole OS crash? Of course not, so allow objects to decide how to handle messages themselves. This is a place where objects shine. Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard were trying to solve a completely different problem. They were interested in simulation. One of the case studies in the Simula manual is modeling the spread of infection across a fixed population. The system is completely closed: you have a fixed set of code, you run your simulation, you get your output. For them, message passing isn’t useful. But things like being able to define simulations in terms of other simulations, specialize entities, and model time as a first-class object are incredibly useful. This is also a place where objects shine! So who used objects “right”? That’s not a sensible question. They did different things because they had different problems. Our modern idea of OOP is a synthesis of all their ideas, as well as the ideas of Adele Goldberg, Barbara Liskov, David Parnas, Bertrand Meyer, Gul Agha, and many others. But none of them can lay claim to what OOP “really means”. Terms evolve as problems do. tl;dr Interviews done 30 years later are not good primary sources. Update 2025-05-07 I am no longer convinced that Alan Kay invented the term OOP. The first uses of “Object-Oriented Language” (in the context of programming languages) were by Douglas Ross in 1976 and Barbara Liskov that same year. The first use with respect to Smalltalk comes later. This arguably makes Powershell the spiritual successor to Smalltalk. [return]

items.overview:
The article "Alan Kay Did Not Invent Objects (2019)" provides a detailed historical clarification regarding the origins of object-oriented programming (OOP) and the development of key OOP concepts. Contrary to widespread belief, Alan Kay did not invent the concept of "objects"; instead, objects originated with Simula, as explicitly cited in the Smalltalk-72 manual and recognized in the 1981 Byte magazine issue that popularized Smalltalk and OOP. These sources credit Simula with introducing the fundamental ideas of objects, messages, and classes. The persistence of the myth that Kay invented objects is partially due to Kay’s own statements from the late 1990s, where he claimed to have coined the term “objects” and suggested Smalltalk was the first to use them. However, Kay later retracted these claims, and primary sources consistently attribute the invention of objects to Simula and its creators, Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard. Kay did, however, coin the term "Object-Oriented Programming," though even this attribution is now in question, as early uses of “Object-Oriented Language” in programming contexts appear in the work of Douglas Ross and Barbara Liskov in 1976.

The article further examines the evolution and interpretation of OOP, highlighting that early OOP was understood to comprise three main ideas: classes defining protocol and implementation, objects as class instances, and messages as the means of communication. While Alan Kay emphasized messaging as the "big idea" in his later reflections, early documentation and practitioners, such as Dan Ingalls, described OOP in terms of the interplay between objects, classes, and messages, with objects controlling the flow of computation. Smalltalk’s unique contribution was its consistent object model: in Smalltalk, everything—including numbers, errors, classes, and even messages themselves—was an object, and the messaging system was decoupled from object internals. Notably, if a method was missing in Smalltalk-80, the system would return a doesNotUnderstand message by default, allowing for flexible error handling and protocol extension, a departure from Simula’s approach where missing methods resulted in errors. This architecture enabled features such as sending messages to objects written in different languages or transmitting object definitions by unconventional means, underscoring the power and flexibility of message-passing in Smalltalk.

The article situates these technical developments within their respective historical and practical contexts. Smalltalk emerged from Alan Kay’s vision for personal computing, where user empowerment and runtime flexibility were paramount—motivating the need for message passing and late binding to allow dynamic system extension and fault tolerance. In contrast, Simula was designed for simulation, modeling closed systems such as the spread of infection in a fixed population, where different aspects of objects—such as specialization and time modeling—were emphasized. The article concludes that there is no singular “correct” usage of objects; rather, OOP evolved as a synthesis of ideas from multiple contributors, shaped by the specific problems they sought to solve. The persistence of myths and oversimplified narratives in technical history is addressed, with the article urging reliance on primary sources and a contextual understanding of innovation—an approach that remains relevant for contemporary system design and product development.

# Today in Tech: From SSL Stacks to Self-Driving Personalization

## The SSL Stack Dilemma

The most urgent development today concerns the SSL library ecosystem, which is facing what amounts to a crisis. OpenSSL 3.0, released in September 2021, has introduced significant performance regressions in multi-threaded environments while simultaneously deprecating APIs that many projects depend on. This creates a perfect storm for organizations running high-performance infrastructure.

The performance issues aren't minor - they're substantial enough that companies may need to provision additional hardware just to maintain existing throughput levels. This has direct implications for energy consumption, carbon footprint, and operational costs. The timing couldn't be worse, as OpenSSL 1.1.1, which many prefer, is losing maintenance support.

What makes this particularly problematic is that Linux distributions have largely moved to OpenSSL 3.0 despite its limitations, since it's the designated Long-Term Support version. Organizations are now forced to choose between using increasingly unsupported older versions or accepting significant performance penalties.

Alternative SSL libraries like BoringSSL, LibreSSL, WolfSSL, and AWS-LC exist, but each comes with its own compatibility and maintenance tradeoffs. This isn't just a technical implementation detail - it affects everything from TLS protocol support to QUIC adoption, certificate management, and regulatory compliance.

## The Corrective Record on OOP

In lighter but still significant news, there's a 2019 piece debunking misconceptions about Object-Oriented Programming. Contrary to some claims, Alan Kay didn't invent objects - they originated in Simula, which the Smalltalk team explicitly cited as inspiration. Kay did coin the term "Object-Oriented Programming," but the notion that OOP was primarily about message-passing rather than classes and objects appears to be a later reinterpretation.

What's particularly interesting is how the piece contextualizes Smalltalk's innovations within Kay's broader vision of personal computing. The late binding and message passing mechanisms weren't abstract computer science - they were practical solutions to make computers more accessible and resilient. In Kay's vision, users should be able to install new programs without recompiling the OS, and a person "clobbering" sound logic shouldn't crash the entire system.

This stands in contrast to Simula's creators, who were focused on simulation problems where message passing wasn't as critical. The takeaway is that OOP evolved as a synthesis of multiple perspectives addressing different problems, rather than having one "true" definition.

## AI Advances in Few-Shot Learning and Autonomous Driving

Two AI papers caught attention today. First, "Latte" introduces a framework for transferring knowledge from Large Language Models to few-shot tabular learning tasks. Unlike previous approaches that either extract knowledge at test time (creating latency) or rely on text-level knowledge (leading to unreliable feature engineering), Latte extracts latent knowledge during training time.

The key innovation is that Latte enables weighted fusion of information across different feature values while reducing overfitting risk in limited-data scenarios. It's also compatible with existing unsupervised pre-training approaches and can leverage unlabeled samples to overcome limitations imposed by extremely small labeled datasets.

Meanwhile, "PADriver" tackles personalized autonomous driving using Multi-modal Large Language Models. It processes streaming frames and personalized text prompts to perform scene understanding, danger level estimation, and action decisions. The danger level assessment provides an explicit risk reference for potential actions, which corresponds to the preset personalized prompt.

The researchers have also created a benchmark called PAD-Highway based on the Highway-Env simulator, containing 250 hours of annotated video. Their experimental results suggest PADriver outperforms existing approaches and enables various driving modes.

## The Common Thread

What ties today's developments together is a tension between legacy systems and emerging innovations. The SSL stack crisis exemplifies how infrastructure dependencies can create significant challenges when evolving. The OOP history reminder shows how technology narratives get simplified and distorted over time. And the AI papers demonstrate how researchers continue pushing boundaries by transferring knowledge between domains (Latte) and personalizing previously standardized systems (PADriver).

The most actionable insight might be to reassess any critical systems relying on OpenSSL 3.0 for performance-sensitive applications. The performance degradation in multi-threaded environments could be silently affecting operational costs and efficiency.
